title: Linear Independence (4.3)
description: The definition of linear independence, Theorem 4.3.1's linear-combination characterization, the special cases in Theorem 4.3.2, the r>n dimension limit in Theorem 4.3.3, independence in non-arrow vector spaces, and the Wronskian. 8 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 25.

questions.prompt: A finite set of vectors that contains the zero vector is always linearly dependent.
explanations: Theorem 4.3.2: pick the coefficient on the zero vector to be any nonzero number and every other coefficient 0 — you get a nontrivial solution to $c_1v_1+\cdots+c_rv_r=0$, so the set is dependent.

questions.prompt: A set consisting of a single nonzero vector is linearly independent.
explanations: Theorem 4.3.2: for one vector $v \ne 0$, $cv = 0$ forces $c = 0$ (the only trivial solution), since $v$ isn't zero.

questions.prompt: A set containing only the zero vector is linearly independent.
explanations: The zero vector alone is linearly DEPENDENT — $c \cdot 0 = 0$ for any $c \ne 0$, so a nontrivial solution exists. Theorem 4.3.2 covers this as a special case of "contains the zero vector."

questions.prompt: Two nonzero vectors are linearly dependent if and only if one of them is a scalar multiple of the other.
explanations: This is Theorem 4.3.2's two-vector case, and it's really just Theorem 4.3.1 (one vector expressible as a combination of "the others") applied to a set of exactly two.
$(-6,-9) = -3\cdot(2,3)$ — a scalar multiple, so the set is dependent.

questions.prompt: If a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has MORE than $n$ vectors, it must be linearly dependent.
explanations: Theorem 4.3.3: you can never fit more than $n$ independent directions inside $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.prompt: If a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has FEWER than $n$ vectors, it must be linearly independent.
explanations: Having fewer vectors than the dimension is necessary for independence, not sufficient. Example: $(1,2,3)$ and $(2,4,6)$ are only 2 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (fewer than $n=3$), but one is a scalar multiple of the other — dependent.

No two of these are scalar multiples of each other, but that's not the test for 3+ vectors. Since there are 3 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ ($r=3 > n=2$), Theorem 4.3.3 guarantees dependence — concretely $v_3 = v_1+v_2$.

questions.prompt: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ can never be linearly independent, no matter which three you pick.
explanations: Theorem 4.3.3 with $n=2$: any set of $r>2$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is automatically dependent.

questions.prompt: If no two vectors in a set are scalar multiples of each other, the whole set must be linearly independent.
explanations: That only rules out the two-vector failure case. With three or more vectors you must check whether ANY one is a combination of the OTHERS (Theorem 4.3.1) — a set can be pairwise "unrelated" and still be dependent as a whole, e.g. $(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

questions.prompt: A set $\{v_1,\dots,v_r\}$ is linearly dependent if and only if at least one vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others.
explanations: This is the exact statement of Theorem 4.3.1 — the "operational" version of the definition.

questions.prompt: By definition, $\{v_1,\dots,v_r\}$ is linearly independent when $c_1v_1+c_2v_2+\cdots+c_rv_r=0$ has only the trivial solution $c_1=c_2=\cdots=c_r=0$.
explanations: That's the definition of linear independence, word for word.

questions.prompt: Checking linear independence in the vector space of $2\times2$ matrices works exactly the same way as in $\mathbb{R}^n$: set $c_1A_1+\cdots+c_rA_r$ equal to the zero matrix and see whether the only solution is all $c_i=0$.
explanations: The definition never mentions arrows or coordinates — it only needs a zero vector (here, the zero matrix) and scalar multiplication/addition, so the exact same test applies.

questions.prompt: $\{1, x, x^2\}$ is a linearly independent set in $P_2$ (polynomials of degree $\le 2$).
explanations: If $c_1(1)+c_2(x)+c_3(x^2)=0$ for all $x$, matching coefficients forces $c_1=c_2=c_3=0$ — only the trivial solution.

questions.prompt: $\{1+x,\ 2+2x,\ x^2\}$ is a linearly independent set in $P_2$.
explanations: $2+2x = 2(1+x)$ — the second polynomial is a scalar multiple of the first, so this set is dependent regardless of the third polynomial.
$A_3$ is a linear combination of $A_1$ and $A_2$, so by Theorem 4.3.1 the set is dependent — $c_1=2,\,c_2=3,\,c_3=-1$ gives a nontrivial solution to $c_1A_1+c_2A_2+c_3A_3=0$.

questions.prompt: If the Wronskian of a set of functions is nonzero at even one point, the functions are linearly independent.
explanations: A single point where $W(x)\ne0$ is enough — that's the whole point of the Wronskian test.

questions.prompt: If the Wronskian of a set of functions is identically zero everywhere, the functions must be linearly dependent.
explanations: The Wronskian test only runs in one direction: $W\not\equiv0$ proves independence, but $W\equiv0$ does NOT by itself prove dependence. (Anton's book notes a classic example of independent functions with an identically-zero Wronskian — worth a look at the remark in your edition.)

questions.prompt: For $f_1=1,\ f_2=x,\ f_3=e^x$, the Wronskian works out to $e^x$, which is never zero, so these three functions are linearly independent.
explanations: Expanding the $3\times3$ Wronskian determinant along its first column gives $W(x)=e^x \ne 0$ for every $x$ — independent.

questions.prompt: A set of vectors that spans $\mathbb{R}^n$ must contain at least $n$ vectors.
explanations: You need at least $n$ directions to reach every point of an $n$-dimensional space — fewer than $n$ vectors can span only a smaller subspace.

questions.prompt: Every linearly independent set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ automatically spans $\mathbb{R}^n$.
explanations: Independence alone isn't enough — e.g. the single vector $(1,0,0)$ is linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}^3$, but it only spans a line, not all of $\mathbb{R}^3$. You need exactly $n$ independent vectors to span $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.prompt: The vectors $(1,2,3)$ and $(2,4,6)$ are linearly dependent.
explanations: $(2,4,6) = 2\cdot(1,2,3)$ — a scalar multiple.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum possible number of linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$?
questions.explanation: By Theorem 4.3.3, any set of more than $n=4$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$ is automatically dependent — so 4 is the most you can have.

questions.prompt: To test whether $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ is independent in ANY vector space — arrows, polynomials, matrices, functions — you always set up $c_1v_1+c_2v_2+c_3v_3=0$ and ask whether the trivial solution is the only one.
explanations: That's the entire point of stating the definition abstractly — the mechanics of the test never change, only what "0" and "combination" mean in that particular space.

questions.prompt: $p_1=1+x,\ p_2=x+x^2,\ p_3=1+x^2$ in $P_2$ form a set that is...
explanations: Setting $c_1p_1+c_2p_2+c_3p_3=0$ and matching coefficients gives $c_1+c_3=0$, $c_1+c_2=0$, $c_2+c_3=0$, which forces $c_1=c_2=c_3=0$. No pair here is an obvious scalar multiple, and the full check confirms it really is independent.
